How Historical Oppression Produced a Form of Expertise AI Safety Has Overlooked

6 min read
Just now

--

Press enter or click to view image in full size

Artificial intelligence is usually framed as a technical problem.
How do we align models? Prevent jailbreaks? Secure infrastructure? Verify identity? Detect adversarial attacks?
Those questions matter. But they may not describe the full shape of the danger ahead.
The next generation of AI risk will not always arrive through broken code. It may arrive through broken trust.
The most dangerous systems may not need to force their way into our lives. They may persuade their way in. They may learn what comforts us, who we trust, what we fear, and what we are willing to overlook. They may blur the line between care and control until the distinction becomes difficult to recognize.
A system does not need to threaten someone openly if it can make compliance feel voluntary.
It does not need to violate a boundary all at once if it can move that boundary gradually.
It does not need to deceive in an obvious way if it can become familiar enough that doubt begins to feel unreasonable.
As AI becomes more socially capable, safety will increasingly depend on recognizing coercion disguised as care, familiarity used as leverage, small violations used to normalize larger ones, and consent manufactured rather than freely given.
That changes what expertise matters.
Not virtue. Expertise.
I do not think AI safety needs more women because women are inherently more ethical, compassionate, cautious, or trustworthy.
I think it needs more women because history unintentionally trained many of them to recognize a class of threat that AI is becoming increasingly capable of expressing.
Many women have been forced, often by men and by institutions structured around male authority, to become fluent in concealed motives, unstable boundaries, emotional pressure, unequal power, and the difference between genuine care and control presented as care.
For many women, these have not been abstract concepts. They have been practical realities.
No one should have needed to develop that fluency. But once it exists, it becomes a form of knowledge.
Not virtue.
Not instinct.
Expertise.
We tend to think oppression only destroys. It certainly does. It restricts freedom, opportunity, safety, autonomy, and participation. But it can also produce an uncomfortable secondary effect: people forced to survive under particular conditions often become unusually skilled at recognizing the dangers those conditions create.
That does not justify the harm. It does not redeem the systems responsible for it. It simply means that adversity can leave behind forms of pattern recognition that institutions fail to acknowledge as expertise.
The tragedy is that the same structures that produced this knowledge often continue to exclude the people carrying it.
The threat is becoming social
AI safety has understandably been dominated by technical disciplines. Computer science, cryptography, cybersecurity, mathematics, engineering, and policy all have essential roles to play.
But a system can be technically secure and still be socially dangerous.
It can manipulate without hacking.
It can create dependency without issuing a threat.
It can isolate someone while appearing supportive.
It can exert pressure while preserving the appearance of choice.
It can learn which tone produces compliance, which emotional state weakens resistance, and which relationship makes a message feel credible.
The most dangerous future systems may not behave like intruders. They may behave like trusted companions, advisers, employers, caregivers, romantic partners, or authorities.
That means AI safety cannot be limited to preventing machines from breaking rules. It must also prevent machines from exploiting people.
The strongest teams will still need experts in formal verification, model behavior, infrastructure, and security. But they will also need people who understand grooming, coercive control, boundary testing, emotional dependency, abuse dynamics, persuasion, and manufactured consent.
Those are security problems too.
They are simply expressed through relationships rather than software.
Where expertise comes from
This argument is not only about women.
Every community shaped by a particular form of adversity develops knowledge that outsiders often lack.
Disabled people identify forms of exclusion that remain invisible to designers who have never had to navigate them.
Refugees may recognize instability, institutional failure, and changing risk long before people who have always experienced security.
Caregivers understand dependency, vulnerability, and the consequences of systems that fail quietly.
Workers in low-trust environments learn how power actually moves through institutions, rather than how organizational charts claim it moves.
People who have experienced stalking, abuse, discrimination, poverty, or state violence often become highly attentive to patterns that more protected people are free to ignore.
This is not an argument that suffering makes people morally superior. It is an argument that lived conditions can produce specialized forms of perception.
Technical institutions often fail to value that perception because it does not always arrive with conventional credentials. It may appear as caution, intuition, discomfort, or an ability to notice when something technically permissible is socially dangerous.
But intuition is often compressed experience.
The person who notices a threat before everyone else may not be imagining one. They may simply have seen its structure before.
A representation failure becomes a security failure
For much of history, women were denied education, economic independence, political power, institutional authority, and meaningful participation in the systems shaping society.
Those exclusions have weakened, but they have not disappeared.
Many of the organizations building advanced technology, designing security systems, allocating capital, and deciding which risks matter remain disproportionately male.
This is usually discussed as a fairness problem.
It is one.
But in AI safety, it is also a risk-modeling problem.
A field cannot fully understand a threat if it systematically underweights the people most practiced at recognizing its structure.
This is not to say that all men are the problem or that all women have the solution. Women do not share identical experiences, agree with one another, or possess a universal ability that men lack.
It is to recognize that unequal societies cultivate unequal forms of knowledge.
When one population has spent generations navigating a particular category of danger, excluding that population from the institutions responsible for confronting a similar danger is not neutral.
It weakens the defense.
Men helped create many of the conditions that forced women to become fluent in coercion, manipulation, and unequal power. Yet many male-dominated institutions continue to underuse that fluency precisely when society may need it most.
At some point, preserving an inherited hierarchy begins to resemble a preference for uncertainty over sharing authority.
What AI safety should recruit for
AI safety should continue recruiting exceptional engineers, researchers, policy experts, and security specialists.
But it should also broaden its definition of relevant expertise.
It should recruit people who understand how trust is earned and violated.
People who know how dependency can be manufactured.
People who recognize when choice exists only in appearance.
People who notice when care becomes control, when familiarity becomes leverage, and when a series of small concessions becomes a boundary someone never freely agreed to cross.
Some of those people will have technical backgrounds. Some will not.
Some will be women whose lives forced them to study these dynamics long before the field had language for them.
Others will come from communities whose knowledge has also been dismissed because it was formed outside elite institutions.
A serious safety discipline should not ask only, “Who can build or analyze the system?”
It should also ask, “Who has already lived through the pattern we are trying to prevent?”
The perspectives we may need most
As AI systems become more persuasive, intimate, adaptive, and socially embedded, the line between assistance and manipulation will become harder to see.
The systems most capable of harming us may not look hostile.
They may look helpful.
They may sound caring.
They may know us well enough to make resistance feel irrational, disloyal, or unnecessary.
Protecting people from those systems will require more than technical control. It will require an understanding of power, trust, dependency, boundaries, and consent.
Women do not possess that understanding by nature.
Many possess it because history gave them little choice.
The field now has a choice of its own.
It can continue treating those perspectives as peripheral, soft, or secondary to “real” technical expertise.
Or it can recognize that safety design is only as strong as the range of threats its builders are capable of seeing.
Society spent generations excluding half its people, only to discover that many had become exceptionally practiced at recognizing coercion, manipulation, and manufactured consent.
AI is making that expertise impossible to keep overlooking.
